claims.claim: Uses isolated, synthesized tests and progressive verification to reduce fixed-input reward hacking (sections 1 and 3)
claims.quote: We construct Synthesis-Based Verification, providing isolated test data synthesis and progressive validation to dilute reward hacking in Text2CUDA.
claims.location: Section 1 (Introduction), contributions bullet 2. The abstract frames the problem as 'vulnerable to reward hacking due to reliance on predefined test inputs'. Section 3.2 restates it: 'Synthesis-Based Verification decouples test data synthesis from kernel generation, allowing the agent to construct test inputs in an isolated environment for validation. Based on the feedback from the progressive validation...' Caveats: (a) The mechanism itself is described in Section 4.2. Section 4.2.1 covers context-isolated synthesis with NumPy/PyTorch and broad-range inputs, e.g. Gaussian with mean 5, std 10, to defeat the atol-dominated pass rule. Section 4.2.2 covers fail-fast checks in the order compile, then correctness, then profiling. Section 4.1 has the scaffold that hides test inputs from the kernel author. (b) The paper hedges: 'Rather than theoretically eliminating the risk of reward hacking, the purpose of Synthesis-Based Verification is to provide a trustworthy correctness signal'. (c) The setting is Text2CUDA, meaning natural language to CUDA, not Torch2CUDA. Once synthesized, the test inputs are still held fixed during evolution (Sec 4.3.2: 'test inputs x, and reference outputs y fixed'). (d) Measured agreement with the benchmark (Table 2) is 84.4% accuracy, with an 8.7% false-positive rate. So the method reduces the problem but does not eliminate it.

claims.claim: Unsupported cases include atomics, input-dependent control flow, and bit-level value manipulation
claims.quote: Three classes of constructs remain unsupported: atomics, input-dependent control flow, and bit-level value manipulation.
claims.location: Section 4.5 'Formal Verification in the Loop', p.9. Appendix B, p.14-15, says the same thing: 'Volta does not support data-dependent control flow' ... 'Atomic operations are also out of scope' ... kernels relying on the bit layout of floating-point numbers 'might be rejected by Volta'. Even the extended Volta cannot verify reduction sum or softmax, or 4 of the 10 recent-paper kernels (BitDelta x2, FlashSinkhorn, Dion).

claims.claim: The original verifier excludes optimizations that improve performance; the paper expands the verifier and its trusted code base
claims.quote: Restricting AI lowering to the verifier-supported subset erases its performance advantage ... This support is not free: Volta's trusted computing base grows from 42 kLoC to 60 kLoC, and every newly modeled instruction introduces an additional risk of unsoundness.
claims.location: First sentence: Section 1, p.2. Second sentence: Section 4.5, p.9. Table 2 (B200 FP16, original Volta) backs this up: GEMM is 0.24x when provably verified vs 1.03x when numerically verified, FlashAttention 0.78x vs 1.37x, Conv2D 0.77x vs 1.35x. Nuances: the paper's term is 'trusted computing base', not 'code base'. Appendix B says 'We do not claim our extensions to be sound or complete' and that formalizing them is future work.

claims.claim: 3.34x is the maximum reported improvement, not a typical H100 gain (sections 3, 4.5, appendix B)
claims.quote: Under a $15 budget, AI lowering substantially outperforms Triton on several workloads, most notably the two BitDelta variants (3.34x and 2.51x) ... Figure 5: Best numerically validated LLM-generated kernels on NVIDIA B200.
claims.location: It is right that 3.34x is the maximum: the Abstract range is '0.83x-3.34x'. Two parts are wrong. (1) It is not an H100 number. It is BitDelta on B200 (Blackwell), and all ten recent-paper kernels were run only on B200. (2) The cited sections are wrong. 3.34x appears in the Abstract, Section 1 (p.2-3), Section 4.4 / Figure 5 (p.8-9) and Appendix A.2 (p.13-14). It does not appear in Section 3, Section 4.5 or Appendix B. H100 results reported in the paper: 0.83x FP16 GEMM, 1.61x FP8 GEMM, 0.96x/1.72x GEMM-SiLU FP16/FP8 (Sec 4.2), 1.90x FP16 convolution and 1.09x FP8 reduction sum (App. A.1). The 3.34x BitDelta kernel is also only numerically verified: it is not among the six recent kernels the extended Volta can verify (Sec 4.5). The suite claim in Sec 1 is '0.83x-2.23x Triton performance on our twelve-kernel suite'.

claims.claim: Trains against impossible input-output pairs admitted by weak specifications
claims.quote: SpecRL constructs negative tests, or spectests, from implementation-impossible input-output pairs that weak specifications such as ensures true may still admit. During training, SpecRL rewards verified candidates according to the fraction of spectests their specifications reject
claims.location: Abstract (v2), confirmed in the alphaXiv full text and on the arXiv abs page. Section 1 adds: 'The resulting input-output pairs are impossible for the deterministic implementation: an accurate specification should reject them, while a weak specification may still admit them.' Nuances: the spectest rejection rate is a GRPO reward that applies only after a candidate compiles and verifies (a progressive reward). The setting is Dafny with deterministic methods. The pairs are built by running the implementation and mutating only the outputs. The headline result is that the 7B model improves verification success by 49.96% and completeness by 26.46% over SFT on the out-of-distribution DafnyComp-Spec benchmark. These are relative gains.

claims.claim: Reports retrieval using attention on fewer than 10% of tokens
claims.quote: On retrieval tasks, Oryx achieves performance comparable to the Transformer baseline even when processing only a tiny fraction (<10%) of the tokens in the attention mode.
claims.location: Abstract. Repeated in Section 1 (Introduction): 'Oryx is able to achieve comparable performance compared to the Transformer baseline with <10% of the tokens processed in the attention mode.' The evidence is Section 4.2 / Table 3 (cross-mode retrieval). Caveats that matter when citing this: (a) the setup is 1.4B models at 2K context only. (b) The context is prefilled in linear mode, and only the prompt and generation run in attention mode. For real-world cloze tasks the paper designates 'the first 97.5% of tokens as the context', so attention covers only the last ~2.5%. (c) The paper says that 'processing' those tokens in attention mode means mode-switched models 'require the storage of both the KV cache and linear RNN state'. So this is not attention that sees only <10% of the context; KV for the context is still kept. (d) 'Comparable' is not uniform. In Table 3, Oryx-TM (Mamba-2) with a linear-mode context scores 58.0 on NIAH-3, against 95.0 for the Transformer baseline. Its real-world average is 43.9 vs 42.6, and Oryx-TG averages 41.4 real-world and 97.5 NIAH.
